title: Crafting the Perfect Investment Portfolio in 2025 - Systematic Investor 331

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Crafting the Perfect Investment Portfolio in 2025 - Systematic Investor 331.docx

speakers: Niels Kaastro Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged)
summary: Niels Kaastro Larsen and Alan Dunne cover Germany's slump, why US long yields rose while the Fed cut (real yields, term premium, fiscal worry), and January 2025 trend-following results. They then review AQR papers (Asness 2035 retrospective, Broad Strategic Asset Allocation) and Howard Marks' bubble note. Conclusions: portfolios rely on correlations from the last 20-30 years, constraints (leverage, career risk, complexity) explain underallocation to alternatives, and trend following is the 'brakes' that lets investors hold equity risk.

coverage.note: intro/disclaimer; Germany GDP contraction, tariff effect, February election
causes of German decline: gas, China competition, demographics, debt brake; oil not especially high
policy missteps in Germany, China WTO naivety; Musk anecdote
risk is vulnerability not predictability; diversification not needed past 15 years; private-as-diversifier illusion
trend following beta vs alpha; US yield move decomposition (real yields vs inflation expectations)
rate expectations repricing, Sahm rule, term premium, foreign central bank holdings
debt-crisis taxonomy, yields self-limiting, refinancing wall, loss of confidence
currency confidence and yield level; January 2025 trend performance and index returns
Asness 2035 retrospective paper; allocators extrapolate past relationships
stock-bond correlation, gold and dollar, imagine the unimaginable; Marks bubble watch intro
Marks: newness, persistence of leaders, valuations vs forward returns, counterarguments
passive flows, 1995-2000 compounding, cost of exiting early; start of AQR allocation paper
AQR broad strategic allocation: theory vs constraints (leverage, liquidity, career/complexity)
fees and vehicles; building blocks, assumptions (vol, Sharpe, returns)
optimizer outputs, composition of alts matters, leverage via high-vol managers, Sharpe penalty
race car/brakes analogy, bond-heavy allocations, factor concentration
GIC/JPM vs AQR results, tracking error barrier, fiduciary duty and ESG shift
fashion shifts (defence), outro; nothing else actionable

completeness_estimate: 0.91 - first reader covered nearly every macro and allocation idea; missed a few conditions (late-90s easy Fed, rising-rate caveat, leverage result), the trend barometer reading and Niels' debt scepticism; two attribution/number errors.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the bundus bank were saying they could knock 0.6% off growth in Germany
claims.claim: The Bundesbank forecast only 0.1% German growth for 2025 before tariffs, and said Trump tariffs could cut a further 0.6%, making a third consecutive contraction year possible.
claims.testable: partly - forecast, resolvable by GDP data

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they're shaping up to be quite a defining moment for um Germany and maybe even Europe in general
claims.claim: The February 2025 German election could bring a policy change (e.g. fiscal) after a prolonged slump, though European policy normally moves slowly.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Germany really benefited from China growing on one hand and then cheap gas from Russia on the other side on both sides they're getting hit now
claims.claim: Germany's model relied on exporting capital goods to China and cheap Russian gas; both sides turned against it, causing the slump.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: when the gas price went up so much they they were literally um not not unproductive um uneconomical
claims.claim: High gas prices made energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals uneconomical in Germany.
claims.testable: partly - industrial output vs gas price

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: China increasingly competing with Germany in Middle Tech and you know higher value industrial goods
claims.claim: China moved from importing German capital goods to competing in mid-tech and higher-value goods (solar panels, EVs), hurting German exports.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the dependency ratio which is kind of the ratio of workers to dependence that's been creeping higher for the last number of years and it's forecast to grow even more
claims.claim: Germany's rising dependency ratio (fewer workers per dependant) is now biting, with anti-immigration politics limiting the fix.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: German tenure yields okay they're not negative anymore but two and a half percent surely you could borrow a two and a half percent
claims.claim: With debt near 60% of GDP and 10-year yields about 2.5%, Germany has room to borrow for productive investment despite its debt brake.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: if you look at oil oil is not spef specifically high at the moment compared to before uh the Ukraine uh Invasion
claims.claim: Energy prices alone cannot explain the German slump because oil is no higher than before the Ukraine invasion (though gas may differ).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the view was you know Chinese economic growth will will will Propel the country towards more um liberalism
claims.claim: Policymakers in the West assumed China's WTO entry would drive political liberalisation and open markets; instead China became a strong producer closed to foreigners, a forecasting error with trade consequences for Germany.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Germany obviously has you know arguably made errors as well in terms of energy policy you know closing down nuclear uh plants as well
claims.claim: German policy missteps (nuclear closure, fiscal conservatism limiting public investment, weak digitalisation) added to external shocks.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: risk is about vulnerability not predict predictability
claims.claim: Portfolios are built around risks investors have thought of, while the real risk is vulnerability to events they have not considered, so unknown-unknown exposure should be addressed.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we've had 10 to 15 years where you haven't really need us if you haven't bothered with any of that you've got away with us
claims.claim: Diversification and resilient construction went unrewarded for 10-15 years, so many investors skipped them and got away with it.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: they just put the word private in front of your investment and then they think oh this is completely different to what else I have in my portfolio
claims.claim: Investors treat private assets as diversifiers although they hold similar risk, an illusion of diversification.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Trend performance versus uh the S&P it's it's it's largy Alpha because the beta is is close to zero over long term
claims.claim: Trend following has near-zero equity beta over the long term, so statistically its return is alpha, although commoditisation weakens that view.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: the dispersion the returns between managers are very different so if you know how can there be a beta if people are so different
claims.claim: Large dispersion between trend managers' returns is an argument that trend following is not a single beta.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we've had this Rising yields and this unusual situation where the FED of Cut Rate by 1% and long-term yields have risen by 1% give or take a few basis points
claims.claim: Since September 2024 the Fed cut by 1% while long-term US yields rose about 1%, a 'reverse conundrum'.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you say nominal yields have changed by about 1% inflation expectations have probably increased by about a third and then two-thirds of it is down to an increase in real yields
claims.claim: Decomposing nominal yields into real yields and inflation expectations shows two-thirds of the rise came from real yields and one-third from inflation expectations.
claims.indicator: real yield, breakeven inflation, nominal yield

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: rates were expected to be down to I think 3% by the end of this year now are expected to be back to around 4%
claims.claim: Fed funds futures moved about 1 to 1.25 points higher (year-end 2025 from 3% to 4%) as recession fears were priced out, explaining the rise in real yields.
claims.direction: yields up when recession priced out

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the Sam realle got triggered back then that unemployment has just stabilized around 4.1 4.2%
claims.claim: The Sahm rule was triggered in August 2024 but unemployment stabilised at 4.1-4.2% as data improved, so recession fears faded.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: basically reflects supply and demand so if there's very strong demand for bonds term Premia is low
claims.claim: The term premium (unobservable, model-estimated residual) reflects supply and demand for bonds; years of strong demand and savings kept it low.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: about 50 basis points ter Premia is now built in which is more consistent what what we've seen historically
claims.claim: The term premium rose to about 50bp, closer to historical norms, reflecting worries about US deficits and debt.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: foreign Central Bank holdings of treasuries have been declining and they they parking their money on repo has also been declining
claims.claim: Falling foreign central bank Treasury holdings and repo balances suggest the composition of dollar buyers is shifting to short-term speculative money, a warning for bonds and the dollar.
claims.indicator: foreign central bank Treasury holdings, foreign repo pool

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: very often in those instances when you get a really big problem is when you've got big debt and credit growth alongside asset bubbles credit fueled asset bubbles
claims.claim: Big debt crises occur when debt and credit growth combine with credit-fuelled asset bubbles; the current situation is more a fiscal challenge than a credit bubble.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: ironically the higher bond yields go up in the short term the more likely they will reverse back downwards later on because obviously higher bond yields have a direct impact on the economy
claims.claim: Rising yields self-limit: a spike can push the economy into recession, which then relieves the bond market.
claims.testable: yes - yield changes vs subsequent growth

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: there is a hell of a lot of refinancing that's coming um even in 2025 I think it's 10 trillion dollars uh most of it shortterm
claims.claim: About $10 trillion of mostly short-term US debt must be refinanced in 2025, a pressure on yields.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: maybe to some extent I'm a little bit surprised that Equity markets have held up so well given the fact that yields have gone up uh quite a lot
claims.claim: Equities have resisted a sharp rise in bond yields, which is surprising and a vulnerability.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if it comes to that that you have to print a lot of dollars to pay um you know or or the FED has to keep buying treasuries um then at some point you can get a loss of confidence
claims.claim: Excess debt financed by Fed purchases can cause a loss of confidence, showing up as higher domestic inflation or a weaker dollar rather than default.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the question is what level of yields is required to entice people to buy you know US Treasury
claims.claim: The relevant question is the yield needed to attract buyers of Treasuries; yields could go somewhat higher.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: Trend follows will certainly have given up some of the early gains in the fixed income markets
claims.claim: In mid-January 2025 trend followers gave up early gains in bonds as yields cooled after a lower inflation print.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: the yin has found some strength maybe as a as a reaction to the noise is coming from the boj about future uh rate hikes and that also impacted Asian uh equities
claims.claim: A stronger yen on Bank of Japan rate-hike talk hurt Asian equities and trend followers.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you look at kind of 10 year or two-year yields so basically been oscillating in a big range around kind of a central point
claims.claim: Trend followers need a breakout; range-bound yields make trend following painful.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I would guess managers are kind of heavily short now or are decent Siz short
claims.claim: Medium-term trend followers were heavily short bonds, which worked until a correction; this positioning is a crowding risk.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: betat up 50 up 1.25% so far this year uh s gen CT index up about uh almost 1% 93 basis points
claims.claim: January 2025 returns: Beta50 +1.25%, SG CTA +0.93%, SG Trend +0.40%, Short-Term Traders +0.81%, MSCI World ~+1%, S&P 500 TR +0.95%, long Treasury index -0.56%.
claims.indicator: SG CTA, SG Trend, Short-Term Traders, MSCI World

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: public Equity performance uh in the US where you know were a bit more um mundane I think Cash Plus 2% um as valuations kind of adjusted
claims.claim: In Asness' 2035 retrospective, US equities earn cash plus 2%, bonds ~1% real, inflation 3-4%, with private equity and Bitcoin underperforming while multi-strats and liquid alts do well.
claims.direction: US equities mediocre; liquid alts good

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: International equities which a lot of people have been kind of saying you shouldn't diversify from the perspective of us investors for a long time which hasn't worked ends up does work over this 10-year period
claims.claim: In the retrospective scenario international equity diversification finally pays off over ten years after a long time of not working.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: levered equities are still equities even if you only occasionally tell your investors their prices
claims.claim: Private equity is levered equity with infrequently reported prices, so its low measured volatility understates its risk.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they get out a trend following just before it starts to do well but it continues to do well in this tough period
claims.claim: In the scenario trend following continues to do well through a tough decade for equities.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of people are allocated and invested BAS based on um what how things have have have worked uh in the in in the last 20
claims.claim: Portfolios are allocated on relationships that held in the last 20-30 years.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: bonds and equities have been generally positively correlated now that's actually normal in the long run
claims.claim: Stock-bond correlation is positive over the long run; the negative correlation of the last 20-30 years was the exception and portfolios relying on it are exposed.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: gold is going up along with the dollar that's not something we normally see
claims.claim: Gold and the dollar rising together is an unusual relationship breakdown.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it seemed impossible to imagine you know the US not having a strong economy and then obviously you had the dot bust
claims.claim: Past regimes looked permanent until they ended (US strength in 1999-2000, then the dot-com bust and the GFC), so investors should be open to all scenarios.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the word he has is newness you know and when you get something new that is the thing that excites people
claims.claim: Marks argues bubbles are driven by newness with no history to temper enthusiasm, applying to AI and crypto.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: investors are betting on per persistence they're betting on nvidia's persistence
claims.claim: The biggest stocks of one era rarely remain the biggest, as with the Nifty Fifty and 2000, so a bet on current leaders is a bet on persistence.
claims.testable: yes - compare top constituents over time

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it basically shows current valuations that PE versus plotted against them kind of forward 10year returns
claims.claim: The J.P. Morgan chart relating starting P/E to forward 10-year returns implies low (about flat or 2%) S&P returns from current valuations.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I don't hear people saying there's no price too high
claims.claim: Marks' counterargument: sentiment is not at 2000-style extremes (no talk of stocks that must be owned at any price) and the S&P P/E is high but not insane.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: is no price too high for Passive investment flows
claims.claim: Passive flows are price-insensitive, so the 'no price too high' behaviour exists through indexing.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: the S&P was actually compounding at something like 28% 5 years in a row
claims.claim: From 1995 to 2000 the S&P compounded about 28% for five years, so valuation-based exits can miss a long run.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you exited because Greenspan was worried about irrational exuberance you missed a huge
claims.claim: Exiting after the December 1996 irrational exuberance warning missed large gains, as the market rose 20%+ in 1997-1999.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: but if you're trying to following in equities it's keeping you invested
claims.claim: Trend following in equities protects the downside and keeps investors invested, reducing the cost of too much caution.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: real world allocation decisions are largely driven by beliefs and constraints
claims.claim: Mean-variance theory says everyone holds one tangency portfolio levered to risk appetite, but real allocations differ due to beliefs about returns and constraints.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you're say running a private weth portfolio or for it's you know retail investor you know there's no real leverage available
claims.claim: Leverage constraints stop retail and private-wealth investors from levering the optimal portfolio.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it may not be optimal say for uh an endowment for a university or something to hold too much private markets if they have to kind of fund or or pay out
claims.claim: Liquidity needs restrict illiquid allocations.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: uncurated strategies positive expected return combine it with equities improves the sharp
claims.claim: Combining uncorrelated positive-return strategies such as trend following with equities improves Sharpe, yet many do not allocate.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: some people don't have a background in in in features and they say oh that sounds risky or I don't understand Quant or I don't understand time following
claims.claim: Complexity and unfamiliarity are constraints that cause underallocation to trend following.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it's kind of like career risk I guess you know you don't want to to invest in something and then it not work out
claims.claim: Peer, benchmark and career risk deter unconventional allocations.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: some people don't want High management fees some people don't want any performance fees and that can constrain what you can access
claims.claim: Fee preferences and vehicle limits (such as UCITS) restrict the strategies available.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: risk mitigation they actually use Trend following to represent that completely
claims.claim: The AQR paper uses ten building blocks (equities, bonds, credit; commodities, diversifying long/short, risk mitigation via trend following; private equity, real assets, private credit) plus cash.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: private Equity is at 20% volatility so in contrast to public equities
claims.claim: The paper proxies private equity with 1.2x Russell 2000 blended with a private equity index, giving 20% volatility versus about 15% for public equities.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: for Commodities the the long sharp sharp is 024 for risk mitigation as measured by train is 024 which seems very conservative
claims.claim: Assumed Sharpe ratios: alternatives 0.3, commodities 0.24, trend (risk mitigation) 0.24, diversifying long/short 0.36; the trend assumption looks conservative.

correction.issue: The 0.3 Sharpe is for the (traditional) asset classes; the speaker corrected himself from 'alt strategies' to 'for the asset classes it's 0.3'.
correction.fix: Assumed Sharpe ratios: asset classes 0.3, commodities 0.24, risk mitigation (trend) 0.24, diversifying long/short 0.36; the trend assumption looks conservative.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Equity 6.9 you know private Equity 7 and a half risk mitigation 5.4
claims.claim: Assumed long-term geometric returns: equities 6.9%, private equity 7.5%, risk mitigation 5.4%.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: once you uh allow for this broader array of asset classes and and based on the assumptions you get a more Diversified portfolio
claims.claim: With broader building blocks the optimizer gives a more diversified portfolio than 60/40 at the same volatility.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: is it 11% allocation to Commodities 15% to long short and 16% to Trend following um and then coupled with a 12% allocation to private Equity
claims.claim: At 60/40 volatility with 4% tracking error and higher fees the optimizer gives 11% commodities, 15% long/short, 16% trend following and 12% private equity (~54% alternatives).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: putting a number like 20 on ALS misses you know the the most important question early you know what's the composition of the old
claims.claim: The composition of an alternatives allocation (liquid vs illiquid) matters more than the headline percentage.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: another way to do that is to leverage via allocating to higher volatility managers
claims.claim: If borrowing is not possible, investors can lever by choosing higher-volatility managers.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you can easily get to a point where alternatives are you know 40 50% of the portfolio
claims.claim: With reasonable return assumptions alternatives reach 40-50% of the optimal portfolio.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: they're basically penalizing that that that sharp ratio for some of these strategies because of their you know maybe uncertainty about what the true sharp is or because of complexity
claims.claim: Underallocation can be explained by investors haircutting uncertain Sharpe ratios.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the point that investors penalise uncertain Sharpe ratios (and complexity) to explain underallocation is made by Alan Dunne in his C15 monologue, not Niels.
correction.fix: Alan Dunne: underallocation to alternatives can be explained theoretically by investors haircutting the Sharpe ratios of these strategies for uncertainty about the true Sharpe and for complexity.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: from a robustness perspective I can see a case for for blending a number of different strategies
claims.claim: Given uncertainty about true Sharpe ratios, blend several diversifying strategies.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they're kind of more consistent return profiles but the but more positively correlated
claims.claim: Diversifying long/short (incl. multi-strats) has higher assumed Sharpe because of consistent returns but is more positively correlated with equities.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: build portfolios that allows you to drive faster because they have good breaks
claims.claim: Trend following and risk mitigation allow meaningful equity exposure by cutting losses, instead of low-risk diversification that slows returns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: in an inflationary environment uh that is devastating to your portfolio and to the pensions
claims.claim: Bond-heavy allocations (60/40 or 80/20 in bonds, as in parts of Europe) are devastated in inflationary regimes.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: most institutional portfolios are heavily influenced by Equity risk
claims.claim: Institutional portfolios of public equity, PE and private credit load on one equity factor, so the apparent diversification is illusory.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: when you integrate the Hedge Fone Port portfolio that decision into the wider portfolio you end up allocating much more to risk mitigation type strategy
claims.claim: The GIC/J.P. Morgan paper found integrating hedge funds into a 60/40 portfolio favours risk-mitigation strategies over steady strategies already captured by 60/40.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: that points you more towards having that higher weight to risk mitigation alongside your your your growth drivers
claims.claim: AQR's mean-variance approach ignores tails and drawdowns, so a robust view favours more risk mitigation than AQR's blend.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: one of the challenges of getting an off Trend in these biger portfolios is the tracking error that it might lead to
claims.claim: Tracking error to a benchmark is a barrier to allocating to trend.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: someone got into really big trouble for having favored ESG in the portfolio at the expense of returns
claims.claim: Conventional wisdom shifts (ESG), so a fiduciary-duty argument against not allocating to risk mitigation is conceivable.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: five years ago it was certainly not in fashion um to be investing in bullets and bombs
claims.claim: Investor preferences flip unpredictably (defence stocks fashionable now), so benchmark conventions are not stable.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: some people would say well you don't have to really worry about debt and certainly not if you're a reserve currency that just doesn't sit so well with me
claims.claim: Niels rejects the view that reserve-currency status makes US debt irrelevant (comparing it to MMT claims that inflation would not return, which proved wrong) and would not dismiss further rises in bond yields.
claims.testable: partly - debt/deficit vs term premium regressions

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: my Trend barometer has been certainly reflecting that all year U been very strong readings for that
claims.claim: The host's trend barometer gave very strong readings in early January 2025, consistent with a strong start for trend followers, before bond and yen reversals hurt in mid-month.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they get out a trend following just before it starts to do well
claims.claim: In Asness's hypothetical 2035 retrospective the allocator exits trend following just before it starts to perform, illustrating the behavioural cost of abandoning a strategy after poor recent returns.
claims.direction: selling after drawdown loses the recovery
claims.conditions: after a poor run of returns
claims.testable: yes - flows into CTA funds vs subsequent returns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: The Magnificent 7 are incredible companies so their pees could be justified
claims.claim: Marks's counterargument to the bubble case: the Magnificent 7 have established moats and generate huge cash flows, so their high P/Es may be justified.
claims.testable: partly - valuation vs subsequent earnings growth

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: people were expecting uh you know issues with Y2K and the FED kept policy easy so you know if you exited because Greenspan was worried about irrational exuberance you missed a huge
claims.claim: The late-1990s rally continued for three years after the 'irrational exuberance' warning partly because the Fed kept policy easy (Y2K concerns, after the 1998 Asian/Russian wobble); whether today rhymes depends on whether the productivity story is as large as then.
claims.testable: partly - valuation signals conditioned on policy stance

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you allow leverage then you would naturally even at that same level of volatility you would borrow um about 50% and you would ramp up um actually in that instance you would ramp up more fixed income exposures
claims.claim: In AQR's optimisation, allowing leverage at 60/40 volatility leads to borrowing about 50% and adding mostly fixed income (plus other blocks), showing leverage constraints push investors toward higher-risk assets instead of levered diversified portfolios.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: where interest rates are coming down I'm not so sure about when interest rates are coming up
claims.claim: Low-risk 'drive slowly' diversification through heavy fixed income worked while interest rates were falling but is doubtful when rates rise, and its underperformance compounds year after year.
claims.direction: bond-heavy diversification fails in rising rates
claims.testable: yes - bond-heavy portfolio returns by rate regime
